The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice for the normalized periodic torus convention used here. Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$ and let $L>0$ be a period length. Put $\mathbb T_L^d=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)^d$, with normalized Haar measure $d\mu_L=L^{-d}\,dx$; writing $y=x/L$ and $\xi=2\pi y$ identifies this normalized measure with normalized Haar measure on $\mathbb T^d=(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)^d$, the periodic Fourier convention fixed in the referenced Fourier-Sobolev definition. Let $K:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)$ be smooth, vanish outside a compact subset of $B_1(0)$, and satisfy $\int_{\mathbb R^d}K(s)\,ds=1$. For $0<\ell<L/2$, define the periodized kernel

$$G_\ell(r)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z^d}\ell^{-d}K\!\left(\frac{r+Ln}{\ell}\right),\qquad r\in\mathbb T_L^d.$$

For a field $q$ with finitely many real components, each smooth and $L$-periodic, define its filtered field by

$$\overline q_\ell(x)=\int_{\mathbb T_L^d}G_\ell(r)q(x-r)\,dx=L^d\int_{\mathbb T_L^d}G_\ell(r)q(x-r)\,d\mu_L(r).$$

Here $dx$ is the volume measure on one period cell. For any smooth periodic vector field $u:\mathbb T_L^d\to\mathbb R^d$, define the subfilter stress and transfer by

$$\tau_\ell=\overline{u\otimes u}_\ell-\overline u_\ell\otimes\overline u_\ell,\qquad \Pi_\ell=-\tau_\ell:\nabla\overline u_\ell,$$

where $(u\otimes v)_{ij}=u_i v_j$, $(\nabla v)_{ij}=\partial_jv_i$, and $A:B=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}B_{ij}$. When $u$ is divergence-free and satisfies the incompressible evolution used in the resolved-energy balance, the sign convention makes positive $\Pi_\ell$ correspond to loss of resolved kinetic energy through the stress term. With length in metres and time in seconds, $x,L,\ell$ have units m, $u$ has units m s$^{-1}$, $G_\ell$ has units m$^{-d}$, $\tau_\ell$ has units m$^2$ s$^{-2}$, and $\Pi_\ell$ has units m$^2$ s$^{-3}$. The nonnegative-kernel hypothesis is part of this definition; no positivity or transfer-sign property is assigned to signed kernels or sharp spectral cutoffs.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $g:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be injective and $C^1$, with $Dg(x)$ invertible on $U$. Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be compactly supported Riemann integrable and suppose $\operatorname{supp}f\subseteq g(U)$. Define
$$h(x)=\begin{cases}f(g(x))|\det Dg(x)|,&x\in U,\\0,&x\notin U.\end{cases}$$
Then $h$ is compactly supported Riemann integrable and
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(y)\,dy=\int_{\mathbb R^n}h(x)\,dx.$$

Let $a<b$ and $c<d$. Suppose $g,h:[a,b]\times[c,d]\to\mathbb R$ are continuous and, for every fixed $t\in[c,d]$, the function $x\mapsto g(x,t)$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ with derivative $h(x,t)$. Define

$$G(x):=\int_c^d g(x,t)\,dt.$$

Then $G$ is differentiable on $[a,b]$ as a function on that interval and

$$G'(x)=\int_c^d h(x,t)\,dt\qquad(x\in[a,b]).$$

At $a$ and $b$ the derivative is relative and one-sided. The derivative hypothesis is imposed only for interior parameter values; continuity of $h$ supplies its endpoint values.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

A bounded $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ on a nondegenerate rectangle is Riemann
integrable if and only if, for every $\varepsilon>0$, some grid $P$ satisfies
$U(f,P)-L(f,P)<\varepsilon$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space (Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous (Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
(Uniform continuity of a map of metric spaces: one $\delta$ serving every point).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
(Every open cover of a compact metric space has a Lebesgue number: a $\delta > 0$ such that every nonempty subset of diameter less than $\delta$ lies inside a single member of the cover).

Let $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ be bounded on a nondegenerate rectangle and let $P$ be a grid. For each cell $Q_i$, put
$$m_i:=\inf f[Q_i],\quad M_i:=\sup f[Q_i],\quad L(f,P):=\sum_i m_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i),\quad U(f,P):=\sum_i M_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i).$$
The extrema exist as finite reals because each nonempty image is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]], [[lem-sup-unique]]), and the sums use the iterated convention of [[def-multidimensional-grid-partition]].

Since $m_i\le M_i$ and cell volumes are nonnegative, $L(f,P)\le U(f,P)$. Moreover
$$U(f,P)-L(f,P)=\sum_i(M_i-m_i)\operatorname{vol}(Q_i),$$
the sum of cell oscillations weighted by volume ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]).

A **grid partition** $P$ of a nondegenerate rectangle $Q=[a,b]\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is a family, one for each $j<m$, of one-dimensional partitions $a_j=t_{j,0}<\cdots<t_{j,n_j}=b_j$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]]). For a multi-index $i=(i_0,\ldots,i_{m-1})$ with $i_j<n_j$, its cell is
$$Q_i:=\prod_{j<m}[t_{j,i_j},t_{j,i_j+1}].$$
A sum over cells means the iterated recursive sum $\sum_{i_0<n_0}\cdots\sum_{i_{m-1}<n_{m-1}}$ of [[def-finite-sum]]. The **mesh** is $\max_{j<m,i_j<n_j}(t_{j,i_j+1}-t_{j,i_j})$, which exists by [[lem-finite-set-has-max]] and is the largest $d_\infty$-diameter ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]], [[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]).

Refinement is coordinatewise. Coordinatewise union gives a common refinement. The cells cover $Q$ and have pairwise disjoint interiors. Repeated splitting of finite sums and induction on $m$ give
$$\sum_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i)=\operatorname{vol}(Q).$$
These statements include boundary overlaps: boundaries may meet, but interiors do not, and volume splitting is algebraic.

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in Finite sums and finite products, by recursion. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n (The unique embedding of ℚ into an ordered field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)) and let
$\varepsilon \in F$ with $\varepsilon > 0$. Then there is a natural number
$n \ge 1$ such that

$$\frac{1}{n \cdot 1_F} < \varepsilon ,$$

where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of $F$ (Every complete ordered field is Archimedean) and
$1/(n \cdot 1_F)$ is its multiplicative inverse (Field). As is standard
we abbreviate $n \cdot 1_F$ to $n$ and write the conclusion $1/n < \varepsilon$.

This is the **reciprocal form** of the Archimedean property.
Every complete ordered field is Archimedean on its own delivers only the assertion that the canonical
naturals are cofinal, $x < n \cdot 1_F$; the form actually used in analysis, that
the reciprocals of the naturals get below every positive bound, is the statement
above, and it is recorded separately so that no proof has to reconstruct the
inversion step in passing.

derivations.claim: For $r$ in a bounded period cell, a nonzero summand requires $|r+Ln|<\ell<L/2$. Only finitely many integer vectors $n$ meet this bound, uniformly on the cell, so the sum is locally finite there; all its derivatives are locally finite sums as well. Replacing $r$ by $r+Lm$ and reindexing $n$ by $n-m$ proves periodicity, and each summand is nonnegative.

Every continuous integrand used below is supported in a fixed nondegenerate compact box $Q$ (enlarge the support box if necessary). By [F7] and [F8], it is bounded and uniformly continuous on $Q$. Write $V=\operatorname{vol}(Q)>0$ and let $\delta>0$ be a uniform-continuity radius for tolerance $\varepsilon/(2V)$. Choose $N\ge1$ with $1/N<\delta/(2R\sqrt d)$ by [F10], where $2R$ is the side length of a box containing $Q$, and divide each side into $N$ equal parts. Each cell's Euclidean diameter is at most $2R\sqrt d/N<\delta$, so each cell oscillation is below that tolerance. By [F9], the Darboux gap is at most $(\varepsilon/(2V))\sum_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i)=\varepsilon/2<\varepsilon$; the criterion [F6] makes the integrand Riemann integrable. This applies componentwise to the compactly supported kernel factors and their products with the periodic field and its derivatives.

Integrating the periodization over a fundamental cell, local finiteness gives a finite sum of integrals. Translating each cell by $Ln$ partitions the support of $y\mapsto\ell^{-d}K(y/\ell)$, so linearity and translation change of variables turn their sum into $\int_{\mathbb R^d}\ell^{-d}K(y/\ell)\,dy$. Apply [F2] to $g(s)=\ell s$ and $f(y)=\ell^{-d}K(y/\ell)$; the integral is $\int K(s)\,ds=1$.

For $\gamma>0$, the functions $K(s)|s|^\gamma$ and $|\partial_jK(s)|\,|s|^\gamma$ are continuous, bounded, and compactly supported. Step 1.2 makes them Riemann integrable, and their integrals are finite by boundedness on a compact box; the finite maximum over $j$ is finite as well.

With an additional smooth periodic factor $q(x-r,t)$, the same finite-cell translation and periodicity give $\int_{\mathbb R^d}\ell^{-d}K(y/\ell)q(x-y,t)\,dy$. Applying [F2] to $g(s)=\ell s$ changes this to $\int_{\mathbb R^d}K(s)q(x-\ell s,t)\,ds$, proving the Euclidean representation.

On a compact time interval inside $I$ and a compact parameter interval for any coordinate $x_j$, the Euclidean representation has a continuous integrand and continuous parameter derivative on the fixed compact support box of $K$. By [F4] the multiple integral is an iterated integral; applying [F3] to each one-dimensional factor and then [F4] again passes $\partial_t$ and $\partial_{x_j}$ through the integral. Repeating this argument for each spatial derivative gives the stated multi-index identities and continuous derivatives.
Steps 1.1–4.1 establish the kernel, convolution, derivative, and moment claims.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space (Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous (Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
(Uniform continuity of a map of metric spaces: one $\delta$ serving every point).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
(Every open cover of a compact metric space has a Lebesgue number: a $\delta > 0$ such that every nonempty subset of diameter less than $\delta$ lies inside a single member of the cover).

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

Let $a<b$ and $c<d$. Suppose $g,h:[a,b]\times[c,d]\to\mathbb R$ are continuous and, for every fixed $t\in[c,d]$, the function $x\mapsto g(x,t)$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ with derivative $h(x,t)$. Define

$$G(x):=\int_c^d g(x,t)\,dt.$$

Then $G$ is differentiable on $[a,b]$ as a function on that interval and

$$G'(x)=\int_c^d h(x,t)\,dt\qquad(x\in[a,b]).$$

At $a$ and $b$ the derivative is relative and one-sided. The derivative hypothesis is imposed only for interior parameter values; continuity of $h$ supplies its endpoint values.

Let $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ be bounded on a nondegenerate rectangle and let $P$ be a grid. For each cell $Q_i$, put
$$m_i:=\inf f[Q_i],\quad M_i:=\sup f[Q_i],\quad L(f,P):=\sum_i m_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i),\quad U(f,P):=\sum_i M_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i).$$
The extrema exist as finite reals because each nonempty image is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]], [[lem-sup-unique]]), and the sums use the iterated convention of [[def-multidimensional-grid-partition]].

Since $m_i\le M_i$ and cell volumes are nonnegative, $L(f,P)\le U(f,P)$. Moreover
$$U(f,P)-L(f,P)=\sum_i(M_i-m_i)\operatorname{vol}(Q_i),$$
the sum of cell oscillations weighted by volume ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]).

A **grid partition** $P$ of a nondegenerate rectangle $Q=[a,b]\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is a family, one for each $j<m$, of one-dimensional partitions $a_j=t_{j,0}<\cdots<t_{j,n_j}=b_j$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]]). For a multi-index $i=(i_0,\ldots,i_{m-1})$ with $i_j<n_j$, its cell is
$$Q_i:=\prod_{j<m}[t_{j,i_j},t_{j,i_j+1}].$$
A sum over cells means the iterated recursive sum $\sum_{i_0<n_0}\cdots\sum_{i_{m-1}<n_{m-1}}$ of [[def-finite-sum]]. The **mesh** is $\max_{j<m,i_j<n_j}(t_{j,i_j+1}-t_{j,i_j})$, which exists by [[lem-finite-set-has-max]] and is the largest $d_\infty$-diameter ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]], [[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]).

Refinement is coordinatewise. Coordinatewise union gives a common refinement. The cells cover $Q$ and have pairwise disjoint interiors. Repeated splitting of finite sums and induction on $m$ give
$$\sum_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i)=\operatorname{vol}(Q).$$

$$\frac{1}{n \cdot 1_F} < \varepsilon ,$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice required by the normalized periodic torus convention. Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$, $L>0$, $\mathbb T_L^d=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)^d$, and $d\mu_L=L^{-d}dx$. Fix $0<\ell<L/2$ and let $K:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)$ be smooth, supported in a compact subset of $B_1(0)$, with $\int K(s)\,ds=1$. Define $G_\ell(r)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z^d}\ell^{-d}K((r+Ln)/\ell)$ for $r\in\mathbb T_L^d$ and, for every smooth periodic finite-dimensional field $q$, $\overline q_\ell(x)=\int_{\mathbb T_L^d}G_\ell(r)q(x-r)\,dx$. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open time interval and let $u\in C^1(I;C^\infty(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d))$ be any smooth periodic vector field. Define

$$\tau_\ell=\overline{u\otimes u}_\ell-\overline u_\ell\otimes\overline u_\ell,\qquad \Pi_\ell=-\tau_\ell:\nabla\overline u_\ell.$$

For $\delta_su(x,t):=u(x-\ell s,t)-u(x,t)$ and $m_\ell(x,t):=\int_{\mathbb R^d}K(s)\delta_su(x,t)\,ds$, the stress has the exact covariance form

$$\tau_\ell(x,t)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}K(s)\,\delta_su(x,t)\otimes\delta_su(x,t)\,ds-m_\ell(x,t)\otimes m_\ell(x,t).$$

It is symmetric and positive semidefinite at every $(x,t)$.

For the additional conclusions below, suppose $\nu>0$ is a constant kinematic viscosity, $p$ and $f$ are smooth scalar and vector fields on $I\times\mathbb T_L^d$, respectively, and $u$ satisfies pointwise

$$\partial_tu+\nabla\cdot(u\otimes u)+\nabla p=\nu\Delta u+f,\qquad \sum_i\partial_i u_i=0,$$

where $(\nabla\cdot T)_i:=\sum_j\partial_jT_{ij}$, $\nabla\cdot v:=\sum_i\partial_iv_i$, and $\Delta:=\sum_j\partial_j^2$. Here $p$ is pressure per unit mass and $f$ is force per unit mass. In SI dimensions, $x,L,\ell$ are in m, $t$ in s, $u$ in m s$^{-1}$, $p$ in m$^2$ s$^{-2}$, $\nu$ in m$^2$ s$^{-1}$, and $f$ in m s$^{-2}$. 

The filtered field satisfies

$$\partial_t\overline u_\ell+\nabla\cdot(\overline u_\ell\otimes\overline u_\ell)+\nabla\overline p_\ell=\nu\Delta\overline u_\ell-\nabla\cdot\tau_\ell+\overline f_\ell,\qquad \nabla\cdot\overline u_\ell=0.$$

Writing $e_\ell=|\overline u_\ell|^2/2$, the pointwise resolved-energy balance is

$$\partial_t e_\ell+\sum_j\partial_j\!\left(e_\ell\overline u_{\ell,j}+\overline p_\ell\overline u_{\ell,j}-\nu\sum_i\overline u_{\ell,i}\partial_j\overline u_{\ell,i}+\sum_i\overline u_{\ell,i}\tau_{\ell,ij}\right)=-\nu|\nabla\overline u_\ell|_F^2+\tau_\ell:\nabla\overline u_\ell+\overline f_\ell\cdot\overline u_\ell,$$

where $|A|_F^2:=\sum_{i,j}|A_{ij}|^2$. Consequently, for every $t\in I$,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\frac12\int_{\mathbb T_L^d}|\overline u_\ell|^2\,d\mu_L+\nu\int_{\mathbb T_L^d}|\nabla\overline u_\ell|_F^2\,d\mu_L=\int_{\mathbb T_L^d}\tau_\ell:\nabla\overline u_\ell\,d\mu_L+\int_{\mathbb T_L^d}\overline f_\ell\cdot\overline u_\ell\,d\mu_L.$$

The forward-transfer sign convention is $\Pi_\ell=-\tau_\ell:\nabla\overline u_\ell$; this theorem makes no sign assertion for $\Pi_\ell$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice required by the normalized periodic torus convention. Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$, $L>0$, $\mathbb T_L^d=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)^d$, and $d\mu_L=L^{-d}dx$. Let $K:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)$ be smooth, supported in a compact subset of $B_1(0)$, with $\int K(s)\,ds=1$, and let $0<\ell<L/2$. Define $G_\ell(r)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z^d}\ell^{-d}K((r+Ln)/\ell)$ and $\overline q_\ell(x)=\int_{\mathbb T_L^d}G_\ell(r)q(x-r)\,dx$. The locally finite sum defining $G_\ell$ is smooth, nonnegative, and $L$-periodic, and $\int_{\mathbb T_L^d}G_\ell(r)\,dx=1$. For every smooth periodic finite-dimensional field $q$, the filter also has the Euclidean representation

$$\overline q_\ell(x,t)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}K(s)q(x-\ell s,t)\,ds,$$

where $q$ on the right is its periodic lift. If $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is open and each component of $q:I\times\mathbb T_L^d\to\mathbb R^m$ and of its time derivative has continuous spatial derivatives of every order, then the filtered field has the same regularity and, for every spatial multi-index $\beta$,

$$\partial_x^\beta\overline q_\ell=\overline{\partial_x^\beta q}_\ell,\qquad \partial_t\partial_x^\beta\overline q_\ell=\overline{\partial_t\partial_x^\beta q}_\ell.$$

$$M_\gamma:=\int_{\mathbb R^d}K(s)|s|^\gamma\,ds,\qquad N_\gamma:=\max_{1\le j\le d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}|\partial_jK(s)|\,|s|^\gamma\,ds$$

are finite.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
(A continuous function on $[a,b]$ is Riemann integrable, by Heine-Cantor and Riemann's criterion).

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral

derivations.claim: By the Euclidean convolution representation, $\partial_j\overline u_{\ell,i}=\int K(s)\partial_j u_i(x-\ell s,t)\,ds$. Since $\partial_{s_j}u_i(x-\ell s,t)=-\ell\partial_j u_i(x-\ell s,t)$, integration by parts in $s_j$ over a box containing $\operatorname{supp}K$ gives $\partial_j\overline u_{\ell,i}=\ell^{-1}\int\partial_jK(s)u_i(x-\ell s,t)\,ds=\ell^{-1}\int\partial_jK(s)(u_i(x-\ell s,t)-u_i(x,t))\,ds$. Here $K$ vanishes at the box boundary and $\int\partial_jK(s)\,ds=0$; the iterated integration is justified by [F4] and the boundary term is zero by [F3].

By [F1], each stress component is $\tau_{\ell,ij}=\int K(s)\delta_{s,i}u\,\delta_{s,j}u\,ds-m_{\ell,i}m_{\ell,j}$. From [F5], nonnegativity of $K$, and [A1], $|\int K(s)\delta_{s,i}u\,\delta_{s,j}u\,ds|\le A(t)^2\ell^{2\alpha}M_{2\alpha}$ and $|m_{\ell,i}|\le A(t)\ell^\alpha M_\alpha$. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice for the normalized periodic torus convention used here. Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$ and let $L>0$ be a period length. Put $\mathbb T_L^d=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)^d$, with normalized Haar measure $d\mu_L=L^{-d}\,dx$; writing $y=x/L$ and $\xi=2\pi y$ identifies this normalized measure with normalized Haar measure on $\mathbb T^d=(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)^d$, the periodic Fourier convention fixed in the referenced Fourier-Sobolev definition. Let $K:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)$ be smooth, vanish outside a compact subset of $B_1(0)$, and satisfy $\int_{\mathbb R^d}K(s)\,ds=1$. For $0<\ell<L/2$, define the periodized kernel

$$G_\ell(r)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z^d}\ell^{-d}K\!\left(\frac{r+Ln}{\ell}\right),\qquad r\in\mathbb T_L^d.$$

For a field $q$ with finitely many real components, each smooth and $L$-periodic, define its filtered field by

$$\overline q_\ell(x)=\int_{\mathbb T_L^d}G_\ell(r)q(x-r)\,dx=L^d\int_{\mathbb T_L^d}G_\ell(r)q(x-r)\,d\mu_L(r).$$

Here $dx$ is the volume measure on one period cell. For any smooth periodic vector field $u:\mathbb T_L^d\to\mathbb R^d$, define the subfilter stress and transfer by

$$\tau_\ell=\overline{u\otimes u}_\ell-\overline u_\ell\otimes\overline u_\ell,\qquad \Pi_\ell=-\tau_\ell:\nabla\overline u_\ell,$$

where $(u\otimes v)_{ij}=u_i v_j$, $(\nabla v)_{ij}=\partial_jv_i$, and $A:B=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}B_{ij}$. When $u$ is divergence-free and satisfies the incompressible evolution used in the resolved-energy balance, the sign convention makes positive $\Pi_\ell$ correspond to loss of resolved kinetic energy through the stress term. With length in metres and time in seconds, $x,L,\ell$ have units m, $u$ has units m s$^{-1}$, $G_\ell$ has units m$^{-d}$, $\tau_\ell$ has units m$^2$ s$^{-2}$, and $\Pi_\ell$ has units m$^2$ s$^{-3}$. The nonnegative-kernel hypothesis is part of this definition; no positivity or transfer-sign property is assigned to signed kernels or sharp spectral cutoffs.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice required by the normalized periodic torus convention. Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$, $L>0$, and $\mathbb T_L^d=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)^d$ with normalized Haar measure $d\mu_L=L^{-d}dx$. Let $K:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)$ be smooth, vanish outside a compact subset of $B_1(0)$, and satisfy $\int K(s)\,ds=1$. For $0<\ell<L/2$, use the periodized filter

$$G_\ell(r)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z^d}\ell^{-d}K\!\left(\frac{r+Ln}{\ell}\right),\qquad \overline q_\ell(x)=\int_{\mathbb T_L^d}G_\ell(r)q(x-r)\,dx.$$

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval and let $u:I\times\mathbb T_L^d\to\mathbb R^d$ have continuous time derivative and continuous spatial derivatives of every order. Define

$$\tau_\ell=\overline{u\otimes u}_\ell-\overline u_\ell\otimes\overline u_\ell,\qquad \Pi_\ell=-\tau_\ell:\nabla\overline u_\ell.$$

For $0<\alpha<1$, let $A:I\to[0,\infty)$ be measurable and assume that for every $(x,t)\in\mathbb T_L^d\times I$ and every $s\in\operatorname{supp}K$,

$$|u(x-\ell s,t)-u(x,t)|\le A(t)\ell^\alpha|s|^\alpha.$$

Using the finite dimensionless kernel moments $M_\gamma=\int K(s)|s|^\gamma\,ds$ and $N_\gamma=\max_j\int|\partial_jK(s)|\,|s|^\gamma\,ds$, define $C_{d,K,\alpha}:=d^2(M_{2\alpha}+M_\alpha^2)N_\alpha$. Then for every $(x,t)$,

$$|\Pi_\ell(x,t)|\le C_{d,K,\alpha}A(t)^3\ell^{3\alpha-1}.$$

For every compact interval $J\subset I$ with $A^3\in L^1(J)$,

$$\int_J\|\Pi_\ell(\cdot,t)\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb T_L^d)}\,dt\le C_{d,K,\alpha}\ell^{3\alpha-1}\int_J A(t)^3\,dt.$$

Consequently this upper bound tends to zero as $\ell\downarrow0$ when $\alpha>1/3$. At $\alpha=1/3$ it is scale-independent and gives no decay conclusion. With $x,L,\ell$ measured in m, $t$ in s, and $u$ in m s$^{-1}$, the Hölder factor $A$ has units m$^{1-\alpha}$ s$^{-1}$, the moments and constant $C_{d,K,\alpha}$ are dimensionless, and $\Pi_\ell$ has units m$^2$ s$^{-3}$. The estimate is conditional on the stated Hölder increment bound; it neither supplies that bound nor proves an endpoint conservation theorem, a turbulent $4/5$ law, or positive anomalous dissipation.
